procedural_history.originating_court: Court XXXII Additional City Civil & Sessions Judge & Special Judge for CBI Cases in Bangalore (CCH 34)
procedural_history.impugned_order: Order dated 08.05.2015 passed by the Special Judge for CBI Cases in Spl. C.C. Nos. 268/2013, 11, 14, 15, 36, 37, 38, 53 & 54 of 2014, allowing an application under Section 451/457 Cr.P.C. of the State.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The respondents (original applicants) filed Writ Petition No. 18941/2016 and Writ Petition Nos. 19328-19335/2016(GM-MM-S) in the High Court of Karnataka at Bangalore challenging the order dated 08.05.2015. The High Court allowed the Writ Petitions on 04.07.2017, directing the release of the iron ore in favor of the writ petitioners (respondents in the Supreme Court appeal).
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The State, aggrieved by the judgment of the High Court, filed Criminal Appeal Nos. 348-356 of 2018 in the Supreme Court. The State is the appellant, and the original writ petitioners (who sought release of the iron ore) are the respondents.

directions: The order and judgment of the High Court is wholly unsustainable and is hereby set aside.

It shall be open for the respondent to file an appropriate application before the XXXII Additional City Civil and Sessions Judge and Special Judge for CBI Cases, Bangalore (CCH-34), for release of seized iron ore by establishing its existence and its ownership right over the same, which may be considered by Jurisdictional Criminal Court in accordance with law.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in directing the release of seized iron ore by relying on the acceptance of a final report in a criminal case that was unrelated to the proceedings in which the iron ore was actually seized?

facts: Iron ore was seized on March 20, 2010, in connection with a case (Crime No. 189/2010) involving illegal stocking.
In this specific case, a Special CBI Judge, on May 8, 2015, granted the State's application to dispose of the seized iron ore.
The respondents challenged this May 8, 2015 order by filing a writ petition in the High Court.
Separately, there was another criminal case (Crime No. 2/2014) investigated by a Special Investigation Team (SIT).
In this separate case (Crime No. 2/2014), a final report was submitted and accepted by a CBI Judge on December 15, 2015, which was favorable to the respondents.

The High Court, in its judgment, allowed the respondents' writ petition and ordered the release of the iron ore, basing its entire decision on the acceptance of the final report in the unrelated Crime No. 2/2014.
law: Sections 451 and 457 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, govern the procedure for the custody and disposal of property seized by the police pending trial.
application: The Supreme Court found that the High Court made a fundamental error by conflating two distinct and separate legal proceedings.
The iron ore in question was seized as part of the proceedings in Crime No. 189/2010, which led to the trial court's order on May 8, 2015, allowing its disposal.
The final report that the High Court relied upon to order the release of the ore was from a completely different case, Crime No. 2/2014.
The Supreme Court reasoned that the outcome of Crime No. 2/2014 had "no effect or consequence" on the proceedings related to the seizure in Crime No. 189/2010.
Therefore, the High Court's reliance on the acceptance of the final report from the unrelated case was irrelevant and an incorrect basis for its decision.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court was not justified in directing the release of the seized iron ore. The High Court's decision was based on a final report from a criminal case that was entirely unrelated to the proceedings in which the iron ore was actually seized. Because this crucial piece of evidence was irrelevant to the case at hand, the Supreme Court found the High Court's judgment to be "wholly unsustainable" and set it aside.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in directing the release of seized iron ore by relying on the acceptance of a final report in a criminal case that was unrelated to the proceedings in which the iron ore was actually seized?
appellant_arguments: The High Court committed an error by allowing the writ petitions and directing the release of the iron ore.
The High Court's judgment was based on a final report accepted in a criminal case (Crime No. 2/2014) that was completely unrelated to the proceedings in which the seizure order was passed.

The respondent had previously filed an application for release of the same iron ore in the correct criminal proceedings (Special C.C. Nos. 268/2013, etc.) but later withdrew it, indicating they knew the proper forum.

In a subsequent, similar case against the same seizure order, the High Court itself directed another petitioner to approach the jurisdictional criminal court, which is the correct procedure and highlights the error in the current judgment.
respondent_arguments: The provided text does not contain the specific arguments made by the respondent.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A party seeking the release of property seized during the pendency of a criminal case must file an application before the jurisdictional criminal court, not a High Court via a writ petition, and establish the property's existence and their ownership rights over it.
obiter: In a separate writ petition filed by another petitioner against the same trial court order, the High Court had also granted liberty to that petitioner to approach the jurisdictional criminal court to seek the release of the seized iron ore by establishing its existence and ownership rights.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The High Court's decision to release the seized iron ore was fundamentally flawed because it was based entirely on the acceptance of a final report in a criminal proceeding that was completely separate and unrelated to the specific criminal cases (Special C.C. No. 268/2013, etc.) under which the iron ore was actually seized. The High Court incorrectly conflated two distinct legal matters, rendering its judgment unsustainable.
legal_tests_applied: The provided text does not articulate a specific legal test, but applies the fundamental principle that a judicial order must be based on the proceedings and facts of the case at hand, not on the outcome of an unrelated matter.
why_appellant_lost: The High Court's judgment, which was in the respondent's (original writ petitioner's) favor, was based on the erroneous premise that a final report submitted by a Special Investigation Team and accepted on 15.12.2015 governed the release of the iron ore.
The iron ore in question was actually seized pursuant to an order dated 08.05.2015 in a different set of proceedings (Special C.C. No. 268/2013 and others), which the High Court failed to consider.

The respondent's own prior actions, specifically filing and then withdrawing an application for release of the same iron ore in the correct criminal proceedings (Special C.C. Nos. 268/2013, etc.), indicated they were aware of the proper jurisdictional court, undermining their subsequent writ petition.
why_respondent_won: The appellant (the State) successfully argued that the High Court committed a clear error by relying on the final report from an unrelated criminal case to order the release of the seized property.

The appellant established that the seizure order was passed in a specific set of criminal cases (Special C.C. Nos. 268/2013, etc.) and any application for release must be adjudicated within those proceedings, not through a writ petition based on a different case.
policy_considerations: To ensure procedural fairness and provide a proper legal remedy, the Court, while setting aside the High Court's order, explicitly granted the respondent the liberty to file an appropriate application for release of the iron ore before the correct jurisdictional criminal court, allowing their claim of ownership to be considered in accordance with the law.
